προφητεύοντι. ὅρα οὖν εἰ μὴ πρὸς τὴν ζήτησιν ταύτην ἄλλη διαστολὴ τῆς
ἀναγνώσεως ἁρμόζει τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον οὕτως ἔχουσα· εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς
χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν
διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν παραπτωμάτων, κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς
χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει· ἐνθάδε
καταπαύσας τὴν τούτου τοῦ τόπου διαστολήν, ἀπ' ἄλλης ἀρχῆς οὕτως ἀναγνώσεται
τὸ γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐτοῦ,
ὥστε τὸ ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει μὴ ἐφαρμόζειν τῷ γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον
pass_a_gloss: Redemption through his blood is forgiveness of trespasses. Ransom frees captives under enemies; we fell under this age’s ruler and his wicked powers, so we needed buying-out and a redeemer to reclaim us after estrangement. The Savior paid his blood as our ransom; hence redemption through blood and forgiveness. Forgiveness trails redemption and cannot precede it. First leave the captor’s grip; then, outside his hands, receive forgiveness for benefit and, healed of sin’s wounds, work piety and the other virtues. On the riches of grace lavished on us: grasp salvation by grace not works, compare trespasses, and the five-hundred/fifty denarii parable shows who owes more thanks to the remitting master. Present sufferings are not worth the coming glory, so grace’s riches are plain, overflowing on called and elect—especially covenant-aliens and promise-strangers pulled by Israel’s fall from the Father’s kindness into salvation. Still richer appears the overflow on the blessed when one weighs judging angels, things angels long to peer into, and the prayer that all be one as Father and Son are one. That entire grace-wealth, starting, growing, multiplying, either meets a zealous partner stretching alongside, or, if the receiver omits what he can do, grace turns empty toward him. Fall short and grace is void; do your part without gap and say with Paul that grace toward me was not empty. On making known the mystery of his will in all wisdom and insight by the good pleasure purposed for the fullness of times: Origen asks what “all wisdom” and then “insight” are. Wisdom of Jesus begins “All wisdom is from the Lord and with him forever.” One who contemplates visibles and invisibles, sorting each by the wisdom in which God made all—David’s “You made all in wisdom”—beholds all wisdom from the Lord. Yet a hearer still in this body, knowing we know and prophesy in part, may trip on “in all wisdom and insight,” as if the claim is too lavish: Paul and peers get the mystery in wisdom, not in all wisdom while knowing in part. Another punctuation helps: close the prior clause after “lavished on us in all wisdom and insight,” then start fresh with “making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure,” so “in all wisdom and insight” does not govern “making known to us the mystery…
pass_b_english: whom we have the redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses. Redemption—or ransoming—happens for captives who have come under enemies. We have come under the enemies: the ruler of this age and the wicked powers under him; and for that reason we needed redemption and the one who buys us out, so that he might receive us back after we had been estranged from him. So the Savior gave his own blood as the ransom for us; therefore we have the redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses. Forgiveness of trespasses follows redemption; before someone is redeemed, forgiveness of trespasses cannot happen for him. First, then, we must be redeemed and no longer be under the one who took us captive and holds us, so that, freed and outside his hands (so to speak), we may for our benefit be able to receive forgiveness of trespasses and, healed from the wounds of sin, act according to piety and the remaining virtues.

Ephesians 1:8: “according to the riches of his grace which he lavished on us.” The one who has understood what it is to be saved by grace and not from works, and who compares trespass with trespass, would see, according to the parable that speaks of the five hundred and the fifty denarii, who ought to confess more favors to the master who remitted the debt. Still, seeing how the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory about to be revealed to us, one would recognize the riches of God’s grace, and how it overflowed upon the called and elect—especially those alien to God’s covenants and strangers to his promises, drawn by Israel’s trespass from the Father’s kindness toward salvation. Still more would someone contemplate the riches of his grace which overflowed upon the blessed by considering “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” and “things into which angels long to look,” and what is said about all being one—“that as I and you are one, they also may be one in us.” And this whole riches of God’s grace which overflowed upon the saints, supplied from some beginning and growing and multiplying, either has the one who obtains what was said competing in zeal and stretching alongside as far as possible, or, if he falls short of doing all that falls to him as far as he can, makes the grace empty toward such a one. If someone falls short, grace becomes as it were empty toward him; but if he does what is from himself without omission, he may say the apostolic word: “his grace toward me was not empty.”

Ephesians 1:9: “in all wisdom and insight making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him for the stewardship of the fullness of the times.” Origen says: what is “all wisdom,” and after that what is “insight”? Jesus also used the word in Wisdom, beginning from “All wisdom is from the Lord and with him it is forever.” So if someone has contemplated the things seen and what is in them or even outside them unseen, and having parcelled them out by reason examines separately the invisible and the visible by the wisdom with which God has made all things—for David says “You made all things in wisdom”—this person would look upon all wisdom from the Lord. But it is likely that someone, despairing that one still wearing this body can already be in all wisdom and insight, and hearing also “we know in part and we prophesy in part,” will stumble at “making known to us the mystery of his will in all wisdom and insight,” as said more generously than truly. For even if the mystery of God is made known to Paul and those like him in wisdom, it is not made known in all wisdom to one who knows all things in part and prophesies in part. See, then, whether another division of the reading does not fit this inquiry of the passage, as follows: “unto the praise of the glory of his grace with which he graced us in the Beloved, in whom we have the redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, according to the riches of his grace which he lavished on us in all wisdom and insight”—stopping the division of this passage here, and from another beginning reading thus: “making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure,” so that “in all wisdom and insight” does not attach to “making known to us the mystery
